papers.title: Distinct electroencephalography alpha-band rhythms map macroscale brain gradients.
papers.abstract: Brain gradients provide a low-dimensional framework for describing cortical organization, linking functional connectivity, anatomy, development, and transcriptional architecture. Whether this macroscale organization also structures fast electrophysiological dynamics remains less clear. Here we used the longstanding observation that alpha-band activity is not unitary, and that some individuals exhibit multiple alpha peaks, as an entry point for examining cortical gradients in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We analyzed source-reconstructed EEG from 608 adults, comprising 3,255 recordings acquired across eyes-open and eyes-closed rest before and after cognitive testing. Within individuals, parcel-wise alpha peak frequencies frequently departed from unimodality, revealing 2 separable alpha-frequency components in 38.3% of recordings. These components were not spatially arbitrary: frequency-defined clusters aligned with canonical functional networks, most prominently separating visual and somatomotor systems, although their relative frequency ordering varied across individuals. Low-dimensional analysis of cluster network composition further identified 2 principal axes: a sensory-differentiation axis contrasting visual and somatomotor contributions, and a sensorimotor-association axis resembling established functional-connectomic gradients. These findings suggest that split alpha reflects multiple sensory-anchored oscillatory modes embedded within macroscale cortical gradients, linking a classical EEG phenomenon to the brain's hierarchical architecture.

papers.title: AcNR1F orchestrates epidermal remodeling to enable host adaptation in Angiostrongylus cantonensis.
papers.abstract: Nuclear receptor NR1F regulates circadian rhythms in mammals, metamorphosis in insects, and molting in free-living Caenorhabditis elegans; however, its role in parasitic nematode development remains elusive. Angiostrongylus cantonensis, a zoonotic pathogen that causes eosinophilic meningitis in humans, exhibits distinct host adaptation, with mice and most mammals serving as non-permissive hosts and rats as the permissive host. We combined multi-omic analyses, lentivirus-mediated RNAi, LC-MS/MS, and dual-luciferase assays to elucidate AcNR1F functions in development and host adaptation. Acnr1f was expressed in the intestine, uterus, and seminal vesicle by in situ hybridization. Acnr1f showed high expression in L5 larvae and adults but low expression in L1-L4 larvae. Acnr1f expression was significantly higher in worms derived from rats than from mice; approximately 25% of co-expressed genes (918) were identified as potential downstream targets that may be integrated to regulate parasitic adaptation. RNAi reduced Acnr1f transcripts by 38.11% in female adults, resulting in significantly decreased recovery of L4 and L5 larvae and adults, a 64% reduction in egg production, and abnormal eggs with low hatching rate. Histological and ultrastructural analyses revealed thinned cuticle, reduced collagen fibers, and disrupted epidermal integrity. Transcriptomic analysis showed that differentially expressed genes were enriched in structural constituent of cuticle, metalloendopeptidase activity, extracellular matrix structural constituent. Dual-luciferase assays showed that the down-regulated collagen genes col-12 and col-144 were direct AcNR1F targets (>300-fold and >40-fold induction, respectively). Differential levels of cholesterol, corticosterone, and 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol between worms from rats and mice were identified as AcNR1F ligands by LC-MS/MS and ligand-binding assays. Thus, AcNR1F is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that directly regulates target genes to influence development and reproduction of A. cantonensis. The distinct availability of host-derived ligands and differential AcNR1F expressive level between worms from rodents highlights this receptor as a critical molecular switch for parasitic adaptation, providing mechanistic insights into host-pathogen interactions.

papers.title: Perceived Stress, Sleep Quality, and Their Impact on Glycemic Control Among Type 2 Diabetes Patients in Riyadh: Cross-Sectional Evidence.
papers.abstract: To investigate the relation between Perceived Stress and Sleep Quality with glycemic blood levels in T2DM patients in Riyadh. This cross-sectional study evaluated a total of 309 patients diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study comprised an initial validation and Arabic translation phase involving 160 participants, followed by an analytical phase focusing on 149 adult patients. To investigate impact of psychosocial and metabolic factors on glycemic control (HbA1c), data were collected using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10), alongside clinical metrics such as BMI and dyslipidemia extracted from medical records. A multivariable linear regression model was utilized to identify independent factors associated with glycemic regulation within the local population. The multivariable regression model demonstrated robust explanatory power (Adjusted R2 = 0.726, p < 0.001). Traditional risk factors, specifically elevated BMI (β = 0.448, p < 0.001) and dyslipidemia (β = 0.304, p < 0.001), were significantly associated with higher HbA1c levels. Notably, poor sleep quality emerged as a significant independent factor associated with elevated HbA1c (β = 0.261, p < 0.001), whereas perceived stress did not exhibit a significant correlation. Conversely, physical activity demonstrated a significant protective effect, correlating with lower HbA1c (β = -0.271, p <0.001). Poor sleep quality, rather than perceived psychological stress, is a primary factor independently associated with hyperglycemia in this patient cohort. These findings suggest that standard diabetes care should integrate formal sleep assessments alongside patient care management.

papers.title: Effects of Transcranial Photobiomodulation on Motor Functions in Healthy Individuals: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis study investigated the effects of transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) targeting the supplementary motor area (SMA) on motor performance and neural activity in healthy individuals.MethodsIn a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 60 right-handed participants received active tPBM (850 nm, 60 mW/cm2, 36 J/cm2) or sham stimulation over the SMA for four consecutive days. Motor performance was assessed using a sequential finger-tapping task for both hands. Neural activity was evaluated using quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) at rest.ResultsActive tPBM significantly improved non-dominant hand motor performance compared to sham, with reductions in reaction time and total movement time, and increased accuracy (all p < 0.001 after Bonferroni correction). qEEG showed significant increases in alpha and beta power at C3 and C4 electrodes in the active group (all p < 0.001 after correction). No significant changes were observed in the sham group.ConclusionThese findings suggest that short-term tPBM targeting the SMA can enhance motor performance, particularly of the non-dominant hand, and increase sensorimotor alpha and beta power in healthy young adults. Further research is needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and potential clinical applications.

papers.title: Positive emotional synchrony and intimacy satisfaction: evidence from a multidimensional assessment.
papers.abstract: Emotional synchrony, as an expression of emotional coordination and coherence, is an important indicator of the quality of intimate relationships. However, few studies have systematically examined valence-related differences in emotional synchrony and their implications for relationship satisfaction, and multidimensional evidence remains limited. In the present research, we employed a multidimensional assessment approach that combined behavioural coding, self-reports, and electroencephalography (EEG) hyperscanning to examine the predictive role of emotional synchrony in relationship satisfaction and the mediating role of self-other overlap during actual interactions. Study 1 revealed that positive emotions played a dominant role in emotional synchrony and directly and positively predicted males' intimacy satisfaction, with self-other overlap serving as a partial mediator. Using self-reports and EEG, Study 2 revealed that emotional synchrony/interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) directly and positively predicted intimacy satisfaction in men, whereas its effect on women's intimacy satisfaction was fully mediated by self-other overlap. In summary, positive emotional synchrony positively predicts intimacy satisfaction, which provides empirical support for the understanding of the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying emotional synchrony.

papers.title: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain.
papers.abstract: Hormones mediate inter-organ signaling, which is crucial in orchestrating diverse behaviors and physiological processes, including sleep and activity, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. The pars intercerebralis and pars lateralis in insects represent major hubs that contain neurosecretory cells (NSCs) that produce various peptide hormones. To obtain insight into how hormonal signaling is regulated, we have characterized the synaptic connectome of NSCs in the adult Drosophila brain. Identification of neurons providing inputs to multiple NSC classes implicates diuretic hormone 44-expressing NSCs as a major coordinator of physiology and behavior. Surprisingly, despite most NSCs having dendrites in the subesophageal zone (primary taste processing center), inputs from peripheral gustatory neurons to NSCs are largely indirect. We also deciphered pathways via which diverse olfactory inputs are relayed to NSCs. Using an influence metric, based on a linear dynamical systems approach, we identify enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity compared to other sensory modalities. Further, our analyses revealed substantial inputs from brain descending neurons to NSCs, suggesting that descending neurons regulate both endocrine and motor output to synchronize physiological changes with appropriate behaviors. In contrast to NSC inputs, synaptic output from NSCs is sparse and mostly mediated by corazonin NSCs. We show that both corazonin-expressing NSCs and their downstream synaptic partner DNg27 influence egg-laying. We additionally explore putative paracrine interconnectivity between NSC classes and peptide hormone pathways from NSCs to peripheral tissues by analyzing single-cell transcriptomic datasets. Our comprehensive characterization of the Drosophila neurosecretory network connectome provides a platform to understand complex hormonal networks and how they orchestrate animal behaviors and physiology.

papers.title: Characterizing sleep disturbances in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies through natural language processing: A retrospective monocentric study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are frequent but undercharacterized comorbidities in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). We aimed to estimate the frequency, spectrum, and burden of sleep disturbances across genetic DEE subtypes using real-world data extracted from electronic health records (EHRs) through natural language processing (NLP). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Dr. Warehouse, an NLP-enabled clinical data warehouse, at a tertiary pediatric center. Data were extracted from January to April 2025. Patients with a group of defined DEEs were identified from narrative clinical notes and matched 1:2 with pediatric neurology patients without history of epilepsy by age, follow-up duration, and document volume. Predefined sleep-related terms were extracted from free-text reports. The proportion of patients with ≥1 documented mention during follow-up was used to estimate occurrence, alongside multivariable logistic regression analyses and a cumulative sleep burden score. The final cohort included 884 patients with DEE and 1280 matched controls. At least one sleep-related disturbance was documented in 63.7% of DEE patients, significantly higher than in controls. The most frequent terms were "sleep disorder," "nocturnal seizures," and "night awakenings." Marked heterogeneity emerged across DEE subtypes; SYNGAP1-DEE showed the highest frequency of sleep disorders, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome was strongly associated with nocturnal seizures, and KCNT1- and PCDH19-DEE were more frequently associated with sleep apnea. DEE patients also exhibited a significantly higher cumulative burden of sleep disturbances compared with controls, with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome showing the greatest burden. NLP-based mining of unstructured EHR data enables large-scale characterization of sleep disorders in DEEs, revealing DEE subtype-specific sleep phenotypes. Routine and etiology-informed assessment of sleep disturbances should be integrated into the clinical management of DEEs.

papers.title: Association of BMAL1, CLOCK, and CRY1 gene polymorphisms with metabolic syndrome and glycemic phenotypes: a case-control study in a Turkish population.
papers.abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) comprises cardiometabolic abnormalities that elevate the risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Growing evidence links circadian rhythm disruption to obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and MetS. This study investigated functional polymorphisms in circadian rhythm-related genes and their associations with MetS and key clinical parameters. A total of 200 patients with MetS and 104 healthy controls were enrolled. Genotyping was performed using PCR-RFLP. Univariate and age-adjusted multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate independent genetic risk factors. The GC genotype of the CRY1 rs2287161 polymorphism was found to be significantly more frequent in the MetS group compared with healthy controls (p = 0.009). After adjusting for age in multivariable logistic regression, the CRY1 rs2287161 GC genotype remained a significant, independent factor for MetS (adjusted OR=0.381, 95% CI: 0.175-0.831, p=0.015). No significant differences were observed between the MetS and control groups in terms of genotype distributions of BMAL1 rs7950226 and CLOCK rs1801260 (p > 0.05). Among MetS patients, individuals carrying the BMAL1 rs7950226 AA genotype exhibited significantly higher fasting plasma glucose levels compared with those carrying the GA and GG genotypes (p = 0.039). An altered distribution of the CRY1 rs2287161 polymorphism was observed in this Turkish cohort, with the GC genotype showing an age-independent statistical association with MetS risk. Additionally, BMAL1 rs7950226 variation modulates glycemic parameters within MetS patients, reinforcing the role of core circadian genes in metabolic regulation.

Plasma p-tau217 and neurodegeneration-related biomarkers predict incident cognitive impairment in obstructive sleep apnea: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with cognitive decline, but biomarkers for identifying cognitively unimpaired patients at increased future risk remain limited. We evaluated the prognostic value of plasma biomarkers associated with neuroaxonal injury and Alzheimer's disease-related biology in OSA. In this prospective cohort study, 286 cognitively unimpaired adults with polysomnography-confirmed OSA underwent baseline measurement of plasma NfL, GFAP, p-tau181, p-tau217, Aβ42, and Aβ40 and were followed for incident cognitive impairment. Cox regression, predictive performance analyses, and linear mixed-effects models were used. During a median follow-up of 4.18 years, 68 participants (23.78%) developed incident cognitive impairment. In fully adjusted Cox models, each 1-SD increase in NfL was associated with a 46% higher risk of incident cognitive impairment (HR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.17-1.83, P = 0.001), and each 1-SD increase in p-tau217 was associated with a 58% higher risk (HR = 1.58, 95% CI 1.25-2.00, P < 0.001). When modeled jointly, both NfL (HR = 1.34, 95% CI 1.06-1.69, P = 0.014) and p-tau217 (HR = 1.47, 95% CI 1.14-1.89, P = 0.003) remained associated with incident cognitive impairment. In longitudinal analyses, higher baseline NfL and p-tau217 were also associated with faster annual declines in MoCA scores when modeled jointly (NfL × time: β = -0.10, 95% CI - 0.18 to - 0.02, P = 0.014; p-tau217 × time: β = -0.16, 95% CI - 0.25 to - 0.07, P = 0.001). Adding both biomarkers to the clinical model increased the C-index from 0.72 to 0.81 and the 4-year time-dependent AUC to 0.81; the optimism-corrected C-index was 0.79. Higher plasma NfL and p-tau217 levels were independently associated with incident cognitive impairment and faster longitudinal cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired patients with OSA.

Scalp Topography of Event-Related Potentials Reveals Differences in Audiovisual Speech Processing in Autistic and Non-Autistic Children.
papers.abstract: In our prior work, conventional event-related potential (ERP) responses to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech were found to explain variance in language abilities in autistic and non-autistic children but failed to differentiate autistic children from non-autistic children. This study extends previous ERP analyses of responses to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech in autistic and non-autistic school-aged children to investigate group and condition differences in the strength and topography of the ERP based on data-driven, reference-independent metrics that overcome limitations of conventional ERP analyses. Extant ERP data from 50 5-12-year-old children (25 per group, matched at the group level on age and sex assigned at birth) recorded during a passive task of listening and watching videos of auditory-only and audiovisual speech syllables were analyzed for differences in ERP strength and topography, quantified via global field power (GFP) and global map dissimilarity (GMD), respectively. GFP was significantly reduced for audiovisual compared to auditory-only speech at 245-275 ms post-stimulus. Groups differed in GMD of the ERPs reflecting the difference in response to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech at 139-170 ms post-stimulus, wherein microstates suggested predominantly differential occipital electrode responses. The benefits of audiovisual integration manifest as a facilitation effect (reduced signal strength of the ERP response to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech) across autistic and non-autistic children. Autistic children also display different patterns of activation underlying ERPs in response to audiovisual versus auditory-only speech relative to non-autistic children. Topographic ERP analyses show promise for advancing our understanding of audiovisual speech processing in autism.

papers.title: Fixed-Sequence OFF-to-ON Differences in Low-Beta State Dynamics in Parkinson's Disease: A Paired Source-Space Resting-State EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Resting-state EEG studies in Parkinson's disease (PD) have largely emphasized static power or connectivity, whereas fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session differences may also involve the temporal organization of network states. Paired source-space evidence under such fixed acquisition protocols remains limited. We analyzed 64-channel eyes-closed resting-state EEG in 39 patients with PD contributing paired OFF/ON recordings for the prespecified 90 s primary analysis; 24 also contributed paired 178 s recordings for duration robustness. After individual MRI-based source reconstruction, low-beta (13-20 Hz) dynamic amplitude-envelope connectivity was computed with 2 s windows. Primary endpoints were switching rate (SR) and normalized Shannon entropy (H); fractional occupancy (FO_path) and mean dwell time (MDT_path) of an internally defined OFF-dominant state were prespecified secondary conditional endpoints and are interpreted only as conditional summaries. PD-only linear mixed-effects models quantified the fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session contrast; medication state and session order were necessarily collinear. In the 90 s analysis, the later ON session showed higher SR (β = 3.3224, Holm p = 0.00406) and H (β = 0.06781, Holm p = 0.000749) than the earlier OFF session. FO_path (β = -0.09167, Holm p = 1.08 × 10⁻⁵) and MDT_path (β = -1.05171, Holm p = 0.00524) were lower in the later ON session. The 178 s reanalysis preserved the same directions, although SR and especially MDT_path were more parameter-sensitive across sensitivity analyses. The fixed OFF-then-ON protocol was associated with reproducible within-subject differences in low-beta state dynamics, with the strongest evidence arising from SR and H. Because medication state was perfectly collinear with session order, these findings cannot distinguish medication-specific effects from order-, time-, vigilance-, fatigue-, or adaptation-related influences. FO_path and MDT_path remain conditional summaries tied to an internally defined OFF-dominant state, and MDT was less stable in the 178 s and OFF-only sensitivity analyses.

papers.title: From Computational Models to Clinical Decision-Making in Epilepsy: Bridging the Gap Between Theory and Practice.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most heterogeneous and unpredictable neurological disorders, characterized by complex brain dynamics, significant interindividual variability, and a therapeutic response that is often difficult to predict. Despite major advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and antiepileptic treatments, clinical decision-making still faces major challenges, including precisely localizing the epileptogenic zone, predicting seizures, identifying drug-resistant patients, and optimizing personalized therapeutic strategies. Over the past two decades, computational models have gradually emerged as promising tools for addressing these challenges. Early approaches relied primarily on mechanistic biophysical models aimed at reproducing the neural dynamics and mechanisms of hyperexcitability involved in epileptogenesis. More recently, the rise of artificial intelligence and deep learning has facilitated the development of predictive models capable of leveraging large-scale multimodal data. Finally, the emergence of digital brain twins and adaptive closed-loop systems now paves the way for personalized computational medicine integrating simulation, prediction, and real-time therapeutic intervention. This review provides a critical analysis of the major international initiatives developed between 2004 and 2026, including the EPICLUSTER/EBRAINS, EPINOSTICS, ENIGMA-Epilepsy, NeuroPace RNS, SeizeIT, EpiBioS4Rx, and NeuroVista projects, as well as several translational platforms based on artificial intelligence and biophysical modeling. We evaluate the actual contribution of these models to clinical decision-making in epilepsy, their translational contributions, their methodological limitations, and the challenges associated with their integration into hospital settings. We argue that the future of computational epileptology does not rest on the opposition between artificial intelligence and mechanistic models, but on their convergence within explainable, personalized, and clinically interpretable hybrid architectures.

papers.title: Micro and nanoscale probes for spatiotemporal cell analysis and manipulation.
papers.abstract: Understanding dynamic cellular processes requires technologies capable of probing living cells with high spatial and temporal precision while preserving viability. Conventional approaches, including bulk omics, microinjection, and electroporation, often provide only static snapshots or induce significant cellular perturbation. Recent advances in micro- and nanoscale probes are enabling minimally invasive intracellular delivery, sampling, sensing, and manipulation with unprecedented precision. This review examines the current state of the art in micro and nanoscale probe technologies, including fluidic force microscopy (FluidFM), nanopipettes, open-space microfluidic probes, and nanoneedle arrays. We discuss how these complementary platforms enable controlled delivery of biomolecules, longitudinal molecular sampling, intracellular electrophysiology, electrochemical sensing, and spatiotemporally resolved analyses from single cells to living tissues. We placed particular emphasis on their ability to overcome the limitations of destructive endpoint assays by facilitating repeated interrogation of the same cell, quantitative molecular delivery, and multimodal measurements with subcellular resolution. Finally, we discuss the remaining engineering challenges, including improving throughput, integrating complementary sensing modalities, and advancing these promising technologies into robust platforms for laboratory studies of cultured cells and tissues.

papers.title: Occupational stress and mental health of police officers in Nigeria.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPolice officers are exposed to occupational stressors; however, little attention is given to the effect of the stressors on their mental health and well-being in many low- and middle-income countries.ObjectiveTo determine the prevalence of operational and organizational stressors and the association with psychological well-being and common mental disorders among police officers in Nigeria.MethodsA total of 1224 randomly selected police officers in four states of Nigeria were interviewed. Validated instruments, including the perceived stress scale, police stress questionnaire (operational (PSQ-Op)/ organizational (PSQ-Org), 12-item general health questionnaire (GHQ-12), 9-item patient health questionnaire (PHQ-9), 7-item generalized anxiety disorder scale (GAD-7), Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI), and the alcohol, smoking, and substance involvement questionnaire (ASSIST), were administered. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Student t-test, ANOVA, and linear regression.ResultsThe overall mean scores on the PSQ-Op (4.24 (sd-1.25)) and PSQ-Org (4.20 (sd-1.25)) were indicative of severe stress. The rates of psychological distress were 22.9%, sleep disturbance- 51.8%, depression- 4.7%, and anxiety- 3.1%. Police occupational stress was associated with service location, perceived stress, psychological distress, sleep disturbance, depression, and anxiety symptoms in bivariate analysis. Perceived stress, sleep disturbance and service location remained significantly related to operational and organizational stress in multivariate analysis while PHQ-9 score was associated with PSQ-Op but not to PSQ-Org.ConclusionPolice officers in Nigeria experience an excessive amount of stress related to their work, and this stress is associated with poor mental and emotional health and is determined by the service location.

papers.title: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation (M = 2.14), compared to activity (M = 0.91), followed by wellness (M = 0.66), and sleep (M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.
papers.journal: The American journal of occupational therapy : official publication of the American Occupational Therapy Association

papers.title: Caring for Preterm Infants on Home Oxygen: A Descriptive Qualitative Study of Caregivers' Experiences in Belgium.
papers.abstract: In the Flemish part of Belgium, preterm births and NICU admissions for acute lung diseases have increased. Nearly half of extremely preterm infants develop bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), requiring prolonged oxygen therapy. Oxygen dependency often delays hospital discharge, leading to more infants going home with oxygen. Caregivers, especially mothers, face significant stress and emotional challenges during this transition, worsened by social isolation due to infection fears. To gain a clearer understanding of caregivers' experiences caring for oxygen-dependent infants at home after discharge. Caregivers of infants discharged home on oxygen from the University Hospital Brussels (UZB) between January 2019 and December 2023 participated in semistructured, nurse-administered interviews. Thirteen caregivers participated. Caregivers adapted to complex care routines, use of medical equipment, and shared caring responsibilities. Fear of infections led to parental preventive behaviors that reduced social contacts and increased feelings of isolation, particularly during high-risk viral seasons. Changed family dynamics included disrupted sleep and altered household roles. Despite difficulties, many caregivers stated their shared caregiving strengthened family bonds. Emotional and financial challenges such as income loss and expenses were frequently voiced. These findings highlight the need for comprehensive ongoing support from healthcare providers (in hospital and at home) to address the medical and psychosocial needs to reduce parental stress and social isolation and that assist families adapt to life at home caring for their infant on oxygen.

papers.title: Reclaiming agency: how women build mood, confidence and social connections during perimenopause.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to understand women's lived experiences of perimenopause, with reference to brain fog, mood, confidence and social connectedness, and identify opportunities to promote well-being. A qualitative, exploratory study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 30 midlife women in Australia from culturally diverse backgrounds. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants described perimenopause as a recurring disruption-stabilization cycle rather than a linear decline. Destabilization was often triggered by sleep loss, cumulative life load and symptom variability, shaping appraisals of mood and confidence. Brain fog was experienced as cognitive disruption accompanied by fatigue and self-doubt, commonly worsened by stress, poor sleep and diet. Participants actively engineered stability using individualized, multi-component strategies, including pacing and withdrawal, sleep optimization, physical activity and well-being practices, organizational and compensatory tools, acceptance and reframing, dietary adjustments, leisure and cognitive stimulation, and social support. Social connectedness was recalibrated, with shifts in engagement, mixed experiences of support versus misunderstanding and a strong preference for validating spaces and relationships. Perimenopause was experienced as dynamic yet manageable through structured self-management and supportive contexts. Findings support holistic, multimodal care that integrates symptom management with sleep, behavioral, cognitive and social interventions.
papers.journal: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation. Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks. Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies. Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies. Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

papers.title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
papers.abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.
papers.journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

papers.title: The link between inflammation and autonomic dysfunction in alpha-synucleinopathies - narrative review.
papers.abstract: Alpha-synucleinopathies are a group of disorders characterized by the accumulation of the pathological form of alpha-synuclein. This group comprises Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, and idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Despite sharing a similar molecular basis, these disorders differ in their clinical presentation. Characteristic manifestations include signs of autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, constipation, gastroparesis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction, among others. These symptoms significantly impair patients' daily functioning and are also negative prognostic factors. Currently, research is investigating the link between inflammation and dysautonomic symptoms. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-α, have been found to accompany these symptoms. Notably, in other diseases characterized by chronic inflammation, autonomic dysfunction is also common. In two human studies of dysautonomic symptoms in other conditions, intravenous immunoglobulin therapy was shown to improve these symptoms. Animal studies have shown that other immunomodulatory agents reduce symptom severity. Modulation of inflammation, dietary modification, the use of probiotics and prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are potential therapeutic approaches for these diseases. These approaches offer hope for improving the quality of life of patients with alpha-synucleinopathies. Further research in this area is needed.

papers.title: Longitudinal Sleep Patterns and Risk of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
papers.abstract: Evidence relating sleep characteristics to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) has largely been based on single assessments. We examined whether transitions in a multidimensional healthy sleep score between two assessments were associated with incident T2DM and explored the relationship of the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index to this association. We conducted a landmark analysis among 60,249 UK Biobank participants with sleep assessed at visits 1 and 2. Visit 2 was defined as time zero for follow-up. Sleep pattern transitions were classified according to poor, intermediate, or healthy sleep status at each assessment. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate associations with incident T2DM. TyG analysis was treated as exploratory. During a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 1284 incident T2DM cases occurred. Compared with stable healthy sleep, stable poor sleep was associated with higher risk (hazard ratio [HR], 2.07; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.32-3.27). Baseline-stratified analyses did not show higher risk for improvement from poor or intermediate sleep relative to remaining in the same baseline category. The full-cohort spline showed evidence of nonlinearity (p for nonlinearity < 0.001), and TyG analyses were exploratory. Sleep pattern transitions between the two assessments were associated with incident type 2 diabetes, and the association differed by baseline sleep status. Repeated sleep assessment may complement single-time-point evaluation in understanding the role of sleep in diabetes risk.

papers.title: Deguelin Alleviates Renal Tubular Epithelial Cell Injury in Lupus Nephritis by Inhibiting the PI3K/Akt Signaling Pathway.
papers.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) is one of the most serious complications of systemic lupus erythematosus. Circadian rhythm disorders are related to the pathogenesis of LN. This study aims to identify the core circadian rhythm-related genes in LN and identify the potential natural active compounds for LN treatment. In the present study, cyclin A2 (CCNA2) and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 3 (CDKN3) were identified as the core targets most related to the circadian rhythm of LN. Both of them were upregulated in blood and kidney tissue samples in LN and had high diagnostic efficacy. Deguelin had strong binding capabilities with CCNA2 and CDKN3 proteins. Deguelin could dose-dependently alleviate lipopolysaccharide-induced human kidney-2 (HK-2) cell damage, inhibit cell apoptosis and the release of inflammatory factors, downregulate the mRNA and protein expression levels of core genes CCNA2 and CDKN3, and inhibit the activation of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt signaling pathway. The protective effect of deguelin could be reversed by AKT activator SC79 treatment. In summary, CCNA2 and CDKN3 are core genes related to the circadian rhythm in LN. Deguelin probably alleviates renal tubular epithelial cell injury by modulating the expression levels of core genes CCNA2 and CDKN3, inhibiting the activation of the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, and thus has the potential to become a therapeutic agent for LN.

papers.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
papers.abstract: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: Circadian Timekeeping in the Tropics: Rhythmic Transcriptome and Diurnal Regulatory Networks in Rubroshorea leprosula.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms allow plants to regulate internal processes to align with daily rhythms in the environment. Comparing circadian clocks across environments is essential because latitude-dependent variation in light and temperature imposes distinct selection pressures that shape the evolution and function of circadian timing systems. However, circadian clock studies have largely focused on temperate and subtropical species, leaving transcriptional circadian networks in tropical plants poorly understood. We report the comprehensive circadian transcriptome of Rubroshorea leprosula, a dominant species in tropical rainforests in Southeast Asia. One sapling was sampled every 4 hours over 48-hour period under constant darkness and used for transcriptomic analyses. Only 283 of 20 748 expressed genes (~1.3%) exhibited significant circadian oscillations, with periods strongly concentrated between 23 and 25 hours. Hierarchical clustering revealed 4 temporal clusters with alternate phases of expression and functional specialization. Comparative analysis identified clear orthologs for all major Arabidopsis circadian clock components, with conserved synteny to Parashorea chinensis, a close relative of R leprosula. Time-lagged cross-correlation network reconstruction identified a characteristic circadian topological similarity with Arabidopsis, including coupled morning and evening feedback loops and paralog expansion that maintained overall structure. Peak expression timing of these core clock genes in the tropical tree was largely consistent with that observed in Arabidopsis thaliana. In contrast, Rubroshorea orthologs showed reduced amplitudes and lower coefficients of variation under this single constant darkness, single-individual condition; because dark-induced damping is common across plants, this pattern is consistent with, but does not establish, reduced circadian robustness in R leprosula linked to tropical adaptation. This study lays the molecular foundation for circadian regulation in dipterocarps and offers a system for integrating rhythmic gene expression to ecological function and forest productivity in tropical communities.

papers.title: Time-of-Day Variation in Knee Extensor Strength and Fatigue Is Associated With Circadian Phenotype in Healthy Young Adults.
papers.abstract: Time-of-day variation in neuromuscular performance is well established, but the contribution of circadian phenotype remains unclear. This study examined whether maximal knee-extensor strength and fatigue resistance differ between morning and evening and whether chronotype and actigraphy-derived sleep-timing are associated with diurnal performance variation. Forty-four healthy young adults (21 males, 23 females) completed a randomised-crossover protocol consisting of neuromuscular testing in the morning (0700-0900) and evening (1700-1900). Participants completed 7 days of actigraphy monitoring and the Composite Morningness Questionnaire to characterise behavioural circadian phenotype. Sleep timing was assessed using habitual sleep midpoint (between sleep-onset and wake-time), with night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint used as an index of sleep-timing variability. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) torque, fatigue index, contractions completed, and time-to-exhaustion were assessed during each trial. Baseline MVIC torque was greater in the evening compared with the morning (2.96 ± 0.80 vs 2.85 ± 0.77 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001), with post-fatigue torque also remaining higher in the evening (2.00 ± 0.60 vs 1.84 ± 0.54 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001). Participants demonstrated a lower fatigue-index (32.57 ± 6.99 vs 35.58 ± 6.26%; P < .0001), completed more contractions (37.95 ± 8.29 vs 35.09 ± 7.58; P < .0001), and exhibited longer time-to-exhaustion (6.36 ± 1.51 vs 5.85 ± 1.26 minutes; P < .0001) during evening testing. Chronotype was strongly associated with the PM-AM difference in MVIC torque (r = -.684, P < .0001), explaining 47% of the variance in diurnal performance responses. Neither habitual sleep midpoint (r = -.029, P = .848) nor night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint (r = -.055, P = .721) was associated with performance differences. No significant sex-related differences were observed. Maximal knee extensor strength and fatigue resistance were enhanced during evening compared with morning testing. The magnitude of this response was strongly associated with behavioural circadian phenotype, but not actigraphy-derived sleep-timing. Findings suggest that chronotype influences time-of-day differences in neuromuscular performance and should be considered when evaluating exercise performance.

papers.title: Characterization of 24-Hour Rhythms in Vital Signs in Intensive Care Populations: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms in intensive care unit (ICU) patients are vulnerable to disruption, which may contribute to adverse clinical outcomes. Continuously monitored vital signs offer a unique opportunity to assess 24-hour rhythms in real-world ICU settings. The aim of this scoping review is to systematically map methodological approaches used to characterize 24-hour rhythms in vital signs in ICU populations and to summarize reported associations with patient characteristics, clinical outcomes, or interventions. A systematic literature search was conducted to identify studies that assessed 24-hour rhythms in routinely collected vital signs in adult, pediatric and neonatal ICU patients published between January 2015 and December 2025. Thirty-five studies comprising nearly 288 000 patients were included, with most studies conducted in adult ICUs (n = 32), 3 in neonatal ICUs, and none in pediatric ICUs. Substantial heterogeneity existed in preprocessing strategies, assessment windows, analytical methods, and derived rhythmicity metrics that were used to determine 24-hour variation, as well as in the level of detail with which these were reported. Cosinor analysis was the most frequently used method to characterize rhythmicity, followed by day-night comparisons, and max-min approaches. Across studies, rhythmicity analyses revealed that 24-hour rhythms in vital signs were detectable in ICU patients, although methodological heterogeneity and lack of detail on analytical decisions limit evidence synthesis. In addition, the direction and magnitude of associations between rhythmic properties (such as amplitude or acrophase) and mortality and other clinically relevant outcomes varied considerably among studies. While most, though not all, studies reported that higher amplitudes were associated with mortality, it remains unclear whether this reflects circadian physiology rather than clinical instability. Harmonization of reporting practices and the development of a core outcome set on circadian parameters derived from vital signs in critical care contexts will help to guide future research in this burgeoning field.

papers.title: Vascular brain injury modifies the relationship between sleep duration, cognition, and white matter hyperintensity burden in the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
papers.abstract: Self-reported sleep duration is associated with dementia-risk and vascular brain injury markers, including white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), yet how additional cerebrovascular pathology alters these relationships remains unclear. In a deeply phenotyped cohort (735) including healthy and Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum individuals (subjective and mild cognitive impairment [MCI], dementia [AD], MCI and AD with high vascular burden [+V]), sleep was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Individuals were classified as WMH-only or WMH+ (WMHs with microbleeds, infarcts, or cerebral amyloid angiopathy). Linear models tested interactions between sleep duration, WMH+ status, and diagnostic group on WMH burden and cognition. In MCI+V and AD, WMH+ significantly amplified the association between shorter sleep and greater WMH burden. In AD, longer sleep related to better cognition in WMH+ but worse cognition in WMH-only (exploratory). Additional vascular brain injury modifies how sleep relates to WMH burden and cognition across the AD continuum, highlighting the importance of moving beyond WMHs alone.
papers.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

papers.title: Bothersome and activity-limiting pain in community-dwelling older adults with versus without stroke: a cross-sectional analysis of the National Health and Aging Trends study (2011-2024).
papers.abstract: Stroke and pain are common health challenges among older adults. However, limited research has examined the burden of pain among community-dwelling older adults with a history of stroke in the United States of America (USA). This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of bothersome and activity-limiting pain and examine the association between stroke history and pain outcomes among older adults in the USA. This cross-sectional secondary analysis used publicly available data from Rounds 1-14 of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), conducted from 2011 to 2024. The study included adults aged ≥ 65 years and compared participants with and without a self-reported physician-diagnosed history of stroke. Pain outcomes were derived from standardized NHATS interview data and included bothersome pain and activity-limiting pain. Demographic, clinical, psychological, physical, and sleep-related variables were obtained from the NHATS dataset. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations between stroke history and pain outcomes after adjustment for relevant covariates. Among 12,797 participants, 2,235 (15.71%) had a history of stroke, and 10,562 (84.29%) did not. The prevalence of bothersome pain was higher among participants with stroke than among those without stroke (60.77% vs. 54.66%; p = .003). Similarly, activity-limiting pain was more prevalent among participants with stroke (62.83% vs. 52.00%; p < .001). After adjustment for demographic, clinical, psychological, physical, and sleep-related factors, stroke remained independently associated with bothersome pain (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.02-1.66; p = .034) and activity-limiting pain (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.04-1.38; p = .013). Pain represents a substantial burden among U.S. older adults with a history of stroke. Stroke was independently associated with both bothersome and activity-limiting pain, highlighting the importance of comprehensive pain assessment and management within geriatric stroke rehabilitation.

papers.title: Cardiac fibrosis and heart failure: Metabolic stress, circadian dysregulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling.
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a major risk factor for heart failure and drives a distinct cardiomyopathic phenotype characterized by oxidative stress, metabolic inflexibility, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive myocardial remodeling. Central to this process is cardiac fibrosis, marked by excessive extracellular matrix deposition, increased myocardial stiffness, and impaired mechanotransduction. Emerging evidence identifies circadian rhythm disruption as an under recognized modifier of diabetic cardiac fibrosis. The circadian clock regulates daily oscillations in myocardial metabolism, redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and extracellular matrix turnover, thereby maintaining cardiac homeostasis. However, modern urbanization has introduced chronic exposure to artificial light at night, particularly blue light from digital devices, which suppresses melatonin and desynchronizes central and peripheral clocks. In diabetes, loss of circadian regulation amplifies TGF-β signaling, Rho-A/ROCK-mediated mechanotransduction, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast transformation. Understanding how circadian misalignment accelerates profibrotic remodeling may reveal novel chronotherapeutic strategies to reduce cardiac fibrosis and heart failure risk.

papers.title: Physical Activity and the Association Between Musculoskeletal Complaints and Sleep Quality in Adults and Older Adults From Primary Care: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Musculoskeletal complaints are the leading cause of disability worldwide and are often associated with poor sleep quality. While evidence suggests that physical activity (PA) positively influences both pain management and sleep quality, it remains unclear whether PA influences the association between musculoskeletal complaints and sleep. This study aimed to investigate the association between musculoskeletal complaints and poor sleep quality, and whether PA modifies this association in adults from primary care. This cross-sectional study analysed data from a Brazilian cohort. Musculoskeletal complaints were defined by self-reported diagnosis of osteoarthritis or low back pain. Sleep quality was assessed using the Mini-Sleep Questionnaire. PA was measured using the Baecke questionnaire. Binary logistic regression was used to test the association between musculoskeletal complaints and poor sleep quality. A total of 557 patients were included (mean age 70.0 ± 8.4 years). Musculoskeletal complaints were associated with poor sleep quality even after adjusting for confounders (OR: 2.36 [95% CI: 1.56 to 3.57]). Stratified analyses showed that this association remained statistically significant among physically inactive participants (OR: 2.47 [95% CI: 1.51 to 4.05]), while the estimate among physically active participants was imprecise and included the null value (OR: 2.10 [95% CI: 0.95 to 4.62]). No statistically significant interaction between musculoskeletal complaints and PA was observed (p-value for interaction = 0.552). Musculoskeletal complaints are associated with poor sleep quality. Although stratified analyses suggested different effect estimates according to PA, the formal interaction analysis did not support effect modification by PA. These findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: Evolution of Outcome Assessment in Chronic Low Back Pain Clinical Trials Throughout the 20th and 21st Centuries: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: To identify, map, and synthesise the outcomes reported in patients with Chronic Low Back Pain (CLBP) and describe how these outcomes have changed over time throughout the 20th and 21st centuries. A scoping review was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Four electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, PEDro, and Google Scholar) were searched for clinical trials published between 1975 and 2025. Five independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and categorised reported outcomes into conceptually related domains. Outcomes and measurement instruments were synthesised descriptively and narratively according to four chronological periods. A total of 708 clinical trials met the eligibility criteria. Pain intensity remained the only outcome consistently reported throughout the entire study period. Over time, outcome assessment progressively expanded to include disability, physical function, physical performance, psychological health, quality of life, work-related outcomes, sleep, fatigue, physical activity, healthcare utilization, and patient-reported outcomes. Measurement instruments also evolved from predominantly symptom-oriented scales to standardized multidimensional questionnaires and, more recently, objective digital technologies. Overall, outcome assessment shifted from a predominantly biomedical approach toward comprehensive biopsychosocial evaluation. Outcome assessment in CLBP clinical trials has undergone a marked conceptual evolution over the past 5 decades. These findings support the adoption of standardized, multidimensional, and patient-centred outcome frameworks to improve the methodological quality, comparability, and clinical relevance of future clinical trials.

papers.title: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Effects on Pulmonary Hemodynamics and Left Ventricular Function in Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) are strongly linked to pulmonary hypertension and left ventricular abnormalities, driving cardiovascular issues. OHS, with daytime hypercapnia, affects 10%-20% of OSA patients. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the first-line therapy, but its cardiac effects are inconsistent. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 (RCTs) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS; cohort studies). Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs using random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood) with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Eight studies (574 participants; 2 RCTs, 6 cohorts) were included, showing that CPAP significantly reduced pulmonary arterial pressure (MD = -2.32 mmHg, 95% CI: -3.88 to -0.76, p = 0.004) versus controls. Secondary analyses indicated improved left ventricular diastolic function (early-to-late diastolic mitral inflow velocity [E/A] ratio: MD = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.09 to 0.48, p = 0.004). No significant effects on left ventricular mass index (LVMi) (MD = -2.31 percentage points, 95% CI: -6.38 to 1.77, p = 0.27) or left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (MD = 0.53 percentage points, 95% CI: -1.49 to 2.55, p = 0.61) were found. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness. Funnel plot analysis suggested potential publication bias for pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)/mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP), E/A ratio, and LVEF, while LVMi showed low bias. In adults with OSA or OHS, CPAP reduces pulmonary arterial pressure and improves LV diastolic function, but it does not significantly alter LVMi or ejection fraction. These findings support CPAP as a key intervention to mitigate pulmonary hemodynamic burden and diastolic dysfunction in this high-risk population, while its potential to reverse structural cardiac remodeling requires further study.

papers.title: The biopsychosocial-spiritual impact upon health information managers from exposure to sensitive information within patient records: A qualitative study.
papers.abstract: Health Information Managers (HIMs) routinely work with patient records containing detailed accounts of illness, trauma and death. While the biopsychosocial-spiritual (BPSS) impacts of trauma exposure have been widely documented among clinicians, little is known about the wellbeing of non-patient-facing health professionals who are repeatedly exposed to sensitive patient information. To explore the BPSS impacts experienced by HIMs following exposure to information contained within patient records. A qualitative study informed by grounded theory methodology was undertaken. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 HIMs employed across a range of Victorian healthcare organisations in Australia. Participants were purposively recruited to represent diverse career stages and workplace settings. Interview data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, guided by the BPSS framework. All participants described impacts in at least one BPSS domain, with many reporting experiences across multiple domains. All participants experienced psychological impacts such as empathy, emotional distress, personal resonance, health anxiety, intrusive thoughts, emotional fatigue, desensitisation and positive psychological responses. Three-quarters of respondents experienced spiritual impacts such as existential reflection, moral and ethical appraisal, compassion, helplessness and gratitude. Biological impacts affected over 50% of participants and included somatic (physical) expressions of emotion, sleep disturbances and physical fatigue. Social impacts were least prevalent, affecting only 10% of participants, and included health advocacy within personal networks and social withdrawal. Findings demonstrated that repeated exposure to patient information alone, despite the absence of direct patient contact, was sufficient to influence participants' wellbeing across multiple domains. These findings challenge assumptions that non-patient-facing health professionals, including HIMs, are unaffected by the emotional consequences of patient care and highlight the importance of recognising occupational wellbeing risks associated with indirect exposure to trauma-related material.Implications for health information management practice:Recognition of BPSS impacts should inform workplace wellbeing initiatives and professional support for the HIM workforce. The findings also highlight the need to consider how education and ongoing professional development can better prepare HIMs to recognise and manage the potential wellbeing impacts associated with working with sensitive patient information.
papers.journal: Health information management : journal of the Health Information Management Association of Australia

papers.title: Advances in monitoring the injured brain.
papers.abstract: Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.

papers.title: In preprints - emerging role of circadian rhythms in refractive development and early-life immune regulation.
papers.abstract: This article discusses the preprinted work of Palumaa and colleagues (2026 preprint) as well as that of Li and team (2026 preprint). As preprints, these works have not yet undergone peer review.

papers.title: Bifidobacterium adolescentis SBT2786-induced early-night sleep requires CCHamide-1 signaling in Drosophila ellipsoid body ring neuron circuits.
papers.abstract: We previously identified the sleep-promoting bacterium Bifidobacterium adolescentis SBT2786; however, its molecular mechanism remains unknown. In Drosophila melanogaster, tissue-/region-specific RNA interference (RNAi) targeted the gut-brain neuropeptide CCHamide-1 (CCHa1) and the CCHa1 receptor (CCHa1R). The increase in SBT2786-induced early-night sleep was abolished by systemic CCHa1 and pan-neuronal CCHa1R knockdown. This phenotype persisted after enteroendocrine cell-specific CCHa1 knockdown, suggesting that it is not fully explained by gut enteroendocrine cell-derived CCHa1 alone. Region-specific RNAi revealed that CCHa1R is required in the ellipsoid body (EB), not the fan-shaped body and tested dopaminergic populations. Ring-driver mapping implicated EB ring neuron circuits, including R3-enriched populations, in the SBT2786 effect: CCHa1R knockdown with the 189 years driver abolished the effect, whereas knockdown with drivers labeling R2/R4m populations did not. These findings show that SBT2786-induced early-night sleep requires CCHa1-CCHa1R signaling and EB ring neuron circuits, and is not fully explained by enteroendocrine cell-derived CCHa1.

papers.title: Effect of a Single Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Gastrointestinal Recovery After Laparoscopic Colorectal Cancer Surgery: A Randomized, Outcome-Assessor-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Postoperative gastrointestinal dysfunction (POGD) and Postoperative gastrointestinal intolerance (POGI) remain a critical challenge in abdominal surgery, particularly for colorectal cancer patients undergoing laparoscopic procedures. Current evidence suggests anesthetic agents may influence gastrointestinal recovery, yet the impact of esketamine remains underexplored. This trial aimed to investigate whether intraoperative esketamine administration accelerates gastrointestinal function recovery. In this single-center, randomized, outcome-assessor -blind trial, 104 patients (aged 18-75, ASA I-III) scheduled for elective laparoscopic colorectal cancer surgery were allocated to receive either intravenous esketamine (0.2 mg/kg) or saline (control) 30 minutes before surgery completion. Primary outcome was time to first flatus; secondary outcomes included I-FEED scores, defecation time, oral intake tolerance, and postoperative complications assessed within seven days after surgery. The esketamine group demonstrated significantly shorter time to first flatus (52 [50.25-53.75] vs 60 [58.59-61.41] hours; P < 0.001) and first defecation (87 [81.96-92.04] vs 95 [92.65-97.35] hours; P = 0.04) compared to controls. I-FEED scores were markedly lower (median 1 [0.25-2] vs 2.5 [1-3]; P < 0.001), with reduced nausea (P = 0.001) and abdominal distension duration (P < 0.001). Esketamine also improved postoperative sleep quality, but did not affect hospitalization costs or length of stay. Intraoperative esketamine accelerates gastrointestinal function recovery after laparoscopic colorectal surgery, especially reducing postoperative gastrointestinal intolerance symptoms of nausea and distension while improving early sleep quality. However, no evident benefit was observed in reducing hospital length of stay or patient costs.

papers.title: The Eye-Brain Axis in High Myopia: From Retinal Deformation to Cortical Network Reorganization.
papers.abstract: High myopia is a major cause of irreversible visual impairment and is increasingly recognized as a condition involving interactions between ocular remodeling and central neural systems. This scoping review synthesizes current evidence on structural, functional, genetic, and regulatory links between the eye and brain in high myopia. We systematically searched PubMed and Web of Science from database inception to August 2026, identifying 54 eligible primary studies. The available evidence indicates that high myopia is associated with retinal and optic nerve abnormalities, altered white matter microstructure, occipital cortical changes, and functional reorganization across visual and higher-order brain networks. However, most neuroimaging evidence is cross-sectional, and Mendelian randomization analyses have not provided evidence for a clear causal effect of myopia on brain volumes. Genetic studies suggest modest overlap between refractive error and cognitive traits, whereas educational exposure appears to contribute causally to myopic refractive development. Experimental and observational evidence also supports reciprocal regulation of ocular growth through circadian, dopaminergic, autonomic, and behavioral pathways, although several proposed mechanisms remain incompletely established in humans. Overall, the eye-brain axis provides a useful integrative framework for understanding high myopia, but longitudinal and interventional studies are required to determine causal relationships and evaluate whether neural or behavioral targets can improve clinical outcomes.

papers.title: From localized to long-range: functional connectivity alterations in mild to moderate chronic low back pain patients.
papers.abstract: Mild pain can influence brain function, yet its central neurobiological mechanisms in chronic low back pain (CLBP) remain insufficiently defined. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate localized and long-range functional connectivity (FC) alterations in patients with mild to moderate CLBP using static/dynamic regional homogeneity (sReHo/dReHo) and seed-based FC, and to assess their statistical relationships with clinical pain and psychological metrics. A total of 55 mild to moderate CLBP patients and 39 healthy controls (HCs) underwent 3.0 T resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and clinical assessments, including Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Short-Form of the McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). sReHo and dReHo (sliding window =50 TRs, step size =5 TRs) maps were computed to identify abnormal localized brain regions. Brain regions showing significant group differences were selected as seeds (6-mm spherical regions of interest, ROIs) for whole-brain FC analysis. Statistical comparisons were corrected using Gaussian random field (GRF) theory (voxel-level P<0.005, cluster-level P<0.05). Partial correlation analyses were used to control for age, sex, education, and head motion (Bonferroni-corrected threshold P<0.007). Compared with HCs, patients exhibited significantly reduced sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis (peak t=-4.253, GRF P<0.05), alongside reduced dReHo in the right parahippocampal gyrus (t=-4.796, GRF P<0.05) and left inferior temporal gyrus (t=-3.935, GRF P<0.05). Seed-based FC analysis revealed decreased connectivity between the third cerebellar vermis and right hippocampus (t=-4.678, GRF P<0.05), and increased connectivity between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus (t=4.441, GRF P<0.05). Patients showed significantly higher SAS anxiety scores (25.15±5.01 vs. 23.08±2.18, P=0.008). Correlation analyses demonstrated that sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis was negatively correlated with SAS scores (r=-0.384, P=0.005), whereas FC between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus was positively correlated with SF-MPQ sensory (r=0.381, P=0.006), affective (r=0.386, P=0.005), and total scores (r=0.445, P=0.001). Patients with mild to moderate CLBP exhibit distinct localized and long-range FC alterations within cerebello-hippocampal and cortico-basal ganglia pathways. These neurofunctional changes may contribute to the integration of subjective pain dimensions and comorbid anxiety. Combining static/dynamic ReHo with seed-based FC provides complementary neurobiological insight into how low-intensity chronic pain may affect the central nervous system and highlights the importance of early clinical recognition.
